paras: The lynching of Thomas Gilyard took place in Joplin, Missouri, on the evening of April 15, 1903, when a white mob of several hundred broke into the city jail, took out Gilyard, a 20-year-old Black man charged with killing a policeman, and hanged him two blocks away. The mob then burned houses in the Black district and drove Black residents from the city. The man named as its leader was sentenced to ten years and later acquitted on retrial.

On the night of April 14, Officer C. Leslie was shot dead in the Kansas City Southern railroad yards while trying to arrest several Black men suspected of theft. On the afternoon of April 15, after an armed search, Lee Fullerton captured a wounded Black man at a slaughter house east of Joplin and took him to the city jail.

Hundreds gathered at the jail crying “lynch him,” and City Attorney P. H. Decker pleaded from the steps for law and order. The crowd battered in the east wall, seized the prisoner, and after Decker held it for half an hour, carried him two blocks to Second and Wall streets. Officers and citizens fought the leaders in what the wire reports called a “tug of war” before he was hanged from a pole.

According to the Topeka State Journal, Sam Mitchell climbed the pole to string the rope, and Gilyard denied firing the shot while admitting he had been present. The mob then swept Main Street and stoned, fired on and burned houses in the Black section, five of which burned by the Topeka count. The Topeka Plaindealer said firemen were kept from the flames, and the wire reports said police were powerless as every Black resident was driven out.

After an inquest on April 16, Gilyard was buried at the city's expense. Mayor Trigg organized 500 armed citizens that day amid reports that men from Pierce City would come to join the attack. The coroner's jury held Sam Mitchell, Ed Fields and a man named Barnes for the hanging, and three men were reported indicted.

At Carthage on June 4 Mitchell was sentenced to ten years for adjusting the rope, while Fields and John Barnes awaited trial for burning houses. In November the St. Louis Palladium reported that Mitchell had been acquitted on retrial and that his alibi witness was arrested for perjury.

A Black correspondent wrote that nearly all Black residents were leaving for St. Louis and the Territories. A mass convention of Black citizens of Jasper County condemned Leslie's killing but resolved that the suspect deserved “a full and fair trial” and thanked the officials who tried to stop the mob. By mid-May leading white citizens were said to be offering to rebuild homes, and some who fled had returned.

White papers from Nebraska to Alabama and Utah printed the wire dispatches under headlines such as “Kill and Burn” and “Negroes Will Be Banished.” The Associated Press called the victim a “negro tramp” taken on suspicion, but the Topeka dispatch saw “little doubt of his guilt,” and a June report called him “the negro murderer.” The Birmingham Age-Herald's editorial “Mob Rule in Missouri” called him innocent and accused the North of hypocrisy.

Black papers condemned the lynching and the attack on residents charged with no crime. The Topeka Plaindealer ran “Joplin Thugs Burn Negro Homes” and urged Black families to defend themselves, as did the Western World's editor. The Chicago Broad Ax turned the case against Booker T. Washington, and the Colored American quoted a claim that the mob acted from envy of Black prosperity.

In Missouri, the Professional World called the lynching “another black spot” on the state, and the Sedalia Weekly Conservator quoted an educator who said the police chief smoked a cigar while the jail was battered. The Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the wire narrative, and the Cleveland Gazette and St. Louis Palladium followed the trials.

Joplin and Carthage dispatches cited a bullet in Gilyard's leg matching Leslie's revolver and, in one version, a confession, while the Plaindealer said he died protesting his innocence. The Jasper County resolutions dated the hanging to the 14th, but the same-day Associated Press dispatch places it on April 15.

reader.title: Lynching of Thomas Gilyard
bases: A mob broke into the Joplin jail, took out a man charged with killing a policeman and hanged him (A2, A3, A12); the burning of Black homes and expulsion of Black residents that followed were part of the same night's violence (A2, A3, A11).

Gilyard was taken from the city jail by a mob of several hundred and hanged without trial over the protests of the city attorney (A2, A3); the mob acted on the charge that he had killed Officer Leslie (A2, A12), and a coroner's jury and a Carthage court treated the hanging as a crime (A20, A33).

Independent wire dispatches from Joplin and Carthage (A2, A3, A6), a Black correspondent in Joplin (A18) and Black resolutions from Jasper County (A27) agree on the jail break, the hanging and the expulsion; only the victim's guilt is disputed.

accounts.gist: Gives the fullest narrative, names Gilyard and Mitchell, says Gilyard denied shooting but admitted being present, and concludes there was little doubt of his guilt.

accounts.gist: Held Sam Mitchell, Ed Fields and a man named Barnes responsible for the hanging.

accounts.label: Black correspondent in Joplin
accounts.gist: A crowd broke the jail and lynched a man supposed to be a tramp, then burned homes; nearly all Black residents were leaving.

accounts.label: Jasper County Black convention
accounts.gist: Condemned the killer of Leslie but said the suspect should have been tried; denounced the lynching and expulsion; praised officials who resisted.

accounts.label: Missouri educator (quoted)
accounts.gist: Called the hanging premeditated, before applauding spectators including women, and said officials declined means to stop the riot while the police chief smoked.

framing.detail: Front-page wire stories under headlines such as 'Kill and Burn' and 'Raid Black Quarter' emphasized the riot and treated the victim as the policeman's killer.
Headlines 'Negroes Will Be Banished' and later 'Mob Leader Sentenced' called Gilyard 'the negro murderer' while reporting the punishment of the lyncher.
The Birmingham Age-Herald's 'Mob Rule in Missouri' called the lynching 'wholly inexcusable' and the victim innocent, while using it to rebuke the North for lecturing the South.
Weekly notes said Joplin's reputation was 'at stake' and that many white citizens had tried to prevent the lynching.
Plaindealer and Western World called the mob 'thugs' and 'white ruffians' and urged armed self-defense.
Missouri Black papers called the lynching a 'black spot' on the state and stressed the suffering of innocent residents.
The Afro-American reprinted the wire narrative and the Gazette and Palladium the court reports, with 'Afro-American' substituted in the Gazette.

The same-day AP dispatch dated April 15 ('tonight') is the best evidence; April 14 was the night Leslie was shot.
